pr_body:
##### Summary
This PR extends the BTRFS metrics we collect. 

Closes https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/3341, closes https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/13561, closes https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/14494 .

##### TODO:
- [x] `/sys/fs/btrfs/[UUID]/commit_stats`
Metrics related to commit stats. Two new charts (per BTRFS filesystem) have been added, one showing commits rate (1 dimension) and another one showing timings metrics (3 dimensions):

![Screenshot from 2023-03-03 16-44-14](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5953192/222777836-989b21a4-873c-4a4c-8e48-c90a75501e8c.png)


- [x] `/sys/fs/btrfs/[UUID]/devinfo/[DEVID]/error_stats`
Metrics related to device errors. One new chart has been added (per BTRFS filesystem). One dimension is created per error metric per device, prefixed with the device ID:

![Screenshot from 2023-03-03 16-44-57](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5953192/222778005-b12229c3-f924-4251-b4fc-11158111d6e1.png)


- [ ] `/sys/fs/btrfs/[UUID]/devinfo/[DEVID]/missing`
Won't be added for now, as it doesn't seem to behave as expected (see https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/14494#issuecomment-1452163022)
- [ ] `/sys/fs/btrfs/[UUID]/devinfo/[DEVID]/replace_target`  
Won't be implemented as part of this PR.

##### Test Plan

Install this branch and check if the expected BTRFS metrics are reported for all your BTRFS filesystems and if they are the same as the `/sys/fs/btrfs/*` stats.

##### Additional Information
<!-- This is usually used to help others understand your
motivation behind this change. A step-by-step reproduction of the problem is
helpful if there is no related issue. -->

<details> <summary>For users: How does this change affect me?</summary>
New charts and alarms for BTRFS filesystem stats that will help in debugging errors or preventing filesystem failures. 
</details>
pr_comments: @Ferroin Feel free to test the current state of the PR and if you are happy with the charts I have added, please add descriptions and alerts to them.

Mostly looks good, but there are three things I think we should ideally change here:

- The commit chart is likely to be much more useful if it’s tracking the rate of commits instead of the total number. That would allow users (and alarms) to more easily see when commits are happening, which is the most useful piece of information this chart can provide.
- Similarly, the total commit time should probably be handled incrementally so that users can see how much time is being spent on commits when. The other two commit timing dimensions largely make sense as they are now (functioning essentially as peak detectors)
- For the error rates, the chart and all dimensions should exist even if there are no errors reported. Whether or not it gets displayed is of course up to the dashboard itself, but it needs to exist so that it we can have proper alarms show up for it in the list of configured alarms even if there are no errors (and so that anything scraping the API actually sees it).

Irrespective of those suggestions, I’ll look at getting chart descriptions and a default alarm config for the error counts added either later today or some time Monday.

> as the incremental one didn't align well with all the other metrics (timings etc.) being absolute, due to interpolation. I thought that would confuse users, since it was the only one shown as an interpolated rate.

I see three problems with this being an absolute dimension:

- The absolute number of commits pretty much _never_ matters unless you’re doing highly specialized testing of the filesystem itself and need to confirm that at least one commit happened since you last looked. For 99.99% of users, what actually matters is the rate of commits, and even then mostly just as a way to explain some parts of disk usage patterns.
- For filesystems that have been mounted for a very long time, checking that commits have been happening consistently is much easier to do with an incremental dimension than an absolute dimension (instead of having to just check for a flat line, you have to check the slope and try to estimate how consistent it is).
- An absolute dimension for this will make interpreting aggregate data more difficult, especially when dealing with filesystems that are not mounted all the time.

I also kind of doubt that users will get confused as long as we properly explain that it’s the commit rate in commits per second, but that’s a bit more debatable.

To be clear, the results are similar to the first chart seen in https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5953192/222777836-989b21a4-873c-4a4c-8e48-c90a75501e8c.png , but instead of a single commit being interpolated and spanning 2 collection intervals (e.g. as 0.64 commits on first collection interval and 0.36 commits on the next one), it will only show in the collection interval it happened (e.g. as 1.0 commit on just one interval). 

It's not a flat line, it is still commit spikes when they happen, but without interpolation.

issue_context.title: [Feat]: Enhanced stats for BTRFS.
issue_context.body:
### Problem

BTRFS exposes quite a few metrics under `/sys/fs/btrfs` that we do not report, many of which are of potential interest to users.

Relevant metrics for the filesystem with a UUID of `[UUID]` are:

- `/sys/fs/btrfs/[UUID]/commit_stats`: This file covers a handful of metrics related to BTRFS commit behavior:
    - `commits`: Counts commits on this filesystem since it was mounted.
    - `last_commit_ms`: Indicates how long the last commit took, in milliseconds.
    - `max_commit_ms`: Tracks the largest value of `last_commit_ms` since the filesystem was mounted.
    - `total_commit_ms`: Tracks the total time taken by all commits since the filesystem was mounted.
- `/sys/fs/btrfs/[UUID]/devinfo/[DEVID]/error_stats`: Provides per-device error counters for `[DEVID]` (which will usually be a small integer number). More details on the exact counters here can be seen in https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/3341.
- `/sys/fs/btrfs/[UUID]/devinfo/[DEVID]/missing`: Indicates whether `[DEVID]` is actually present on the system or not. The relevant metric here is how many devices show a value other than 0 in this file for a given filesystem, which is a reliable proxy for whether the filesystem is operating in degraded mode or not (and is therefore something that we ideally should also have an alert for).
- `/sys/fs/btrfs/[UUID]/devinfo/[DEVID]/replace_target`: Indicates whether `[DEVID]` is being used as the target for a device replacement operation. Again, the relevant metric here is how many devices show a value other than 0 in this file for a given filesystem. If one or more devices are active replace targets, then there is an ongoing device replacement operation. This, on it’s own, is not super useful information, but it is useful to inform ML about more specific aspects of system behavior, and can also be used to make alerting a bit smarter if we can reliably map the device ID to the actual device path.

### Description

Collect the additional BTRFS metrics outlined above.

### Importance

really want

### Value proposition

Users will be able to better monitor performance, reliability, and status of their BTRFS volumes.

### Proposed implementation

Special handling may be needed to map device IDs to actual devices.

review_comments: Why absolute? Should we show error rate (incremental)?

As errors indicate corruption or hardware error, I believe users would want to keep them to 0. Once they have fixed the error by repairing the filesystem or replacing a device, they can reset the error counters with something like `btrfs device stats --reset` . @Ferroin what's your opinion?

I agree that absolute makes more sense here than incremental.

For all the error types, the ideal situation is zeroes across the board, and 99% of users will want alerting on any non-zero value, with the alert staying raised until the error count is reset when the issue has been dealt with (we _can_ do this with an incremental chart, but it’s much harder to understand the alerting logic in that case). Additionally, outside of very extreme cases, the norm is infrequent spikes in the number of errors, so tracking the rate is potentially very misleading when there have been no errors recently.

The crucial part to understanding this logic though is the fact that the counters can be reset by hand, and most admins do so after an incident is resolved because it makes it easier to keep track of whether there has been an issue or not (since you can look for any non-zero value instead of having to remember what the values were last time).
